## The Deal

A machine does not make you stronger. It changes how your strength gets used — and it always charges you for the favor.

There are six classic **simple machines**, and everything mechanical you have ever touched is built from them.

A **lever** is a stiff bar that turns on a fixed point called a **fulcrum**. Push down on one end and the other end lifts. A crowbar, a seesaw, a bottle opener, and the bones in your arm are all levers.

An **inclined plane** is a ramp. Walking a heavy box up a ramp takes less force than lifting it straight up — but you have to travel farther to get it to the same height.

A **wedge** is really an inclined plane that moves. An axe, a knife, a nail, and your front teeth all drive a thin edge into something and push it apart.

A **screw** is an inclined plane wrapped around a post. Look closely at the threads — that spiral is a ramp that has been rolled up. Turning the screw many times pulls it forward a small distance with great force.

A **wheel and axle** is a wheel fixed to a rod so they turn together. Doorknobs, steering wheels, and screwdrivers all use it. A small turn at the wide outer edge produces a strong twist at the narrow center.

A **pulley** is a wheel with a groove for a rope. One pulley changes the direction you pull — handy, because pulling down is easier than lifting up. Add more pulleys and you also reduce the force needed, though you must pull more rope.

Now the deal, which is the same in every case: **you trade distance for force.** Use half the force, move twice as far. Use a quarter of the force, move four times as far. A machine never reduces the total work — it just spreads it out into a form your body can manage.

And every real machine charges a small extra fee called **friction**, which turns a bit of your effort into heat. That is why rubbing your hands warms them and why machines need grease.

So when someone says a machine makes work easier, they mean something precise. Not less work. Less force at any one moment, paid for with more distance — a trade that is almost always worth making.

## The Deal

A machine does not make you stronger. It changes how your strength gets used — and it always charges you for the favor.

There are six classic **simple machines**, and many everyday tools combine them.

A **lever** is a stiff bar that turns on a fixed point called a **fulcrum**. In one common arrangement, pushing down on one side of the fulcrum lifts the other side. A crowbar, a seesaw, a bottle opener, and the bones in your arm are all levers.

An **inclined plane** is a ramp. Walking a heavy box up a ramp takes less force than lifting it straight up — but you have to travel farther to get it to the same height.

A **wedge** is really an inclined plane that moves. An axe, a knife, a nail, and your front teeth all drive a thin edge into something and push it apart.

A **screw** is an inclined plane wrapped around a post. Look closely at the threads — that spiral is a ramp that has been rolled up. Turning the screw many times pulls it forward a small distance with great force.

A **wheel and axle** is a wheel fixed to a rod so they turn together. Doorknobs, steering wheels, and screwdrivers all use it. A tangential push at the wide outer edge can produce a larger force at the narrow axle; both turn through the same angle, while the rim travels farther.

A **pulley** is a wheel with a groove for a rope. A single fixed pulley changes pull direction. A movable pulley attached to a load can reduce the effort force. The ideal advantage depends on the rope segments supporting the moving load, not simply on the number of wheels.

Here is the ideal trade when a machine multiplies force: **less effort force means more effort distance.** Half the force requires twice the distance; a quarter requires four times the distance. Some arrangements instead change direction or increase movement speed. Without friction, input work equals output work.

Real machines also have **friction** and other losses, which convert some mechanical energy into thermal energy and other forms. These losses can be small or large. That is why rubbing your hands warms them and why machines need grease.

So when someone says a machine makes work easier, they mean something precise. A machine may reduce the required effort force, change its direction, or change speed. It cannot create energy. For the same useful task, losses make real input work greater than useful output work.

from: Design a simple machine, or a combination of two, that lets one student lift a full five-gallon water jug onto a table using less force than lifting it by hand. Predict the trade you are making, then test it.
to: Design and test a small tabletop model of a machine that could help lift a water jug. Use a sealed container with a total mass no greater than 250 grams as the model load. Raise it no more than 10 centimeters above a tray, with teacher approval. Do not lift a full water-cooler jug.

from: The classroom water cooler sits on a table. Full replacement jugs weigh about 19 kilograms (over 40 pounds), too heavy for most students to lift safely onto the table. You have a sturdy plank, a wooden block, rope, two pulleys with hooks, a hand truck wheel, tape, and a spring scale that reads up to 10 kilograms of pull.
to: A water cooler needs replacement jugs, but a full jug is too heavy for this classroom experiment. Model the problem using a sealed container no heavier than 250 grams, a short ruler or craft plank, blocks, string, small classroom pulleys and a spring scale marked in newtons. Keep the setup on a tray and the rise at 10 centimeters or less.

from: Which simple machine, or pair of machines, lets one student raise the full jug onto the table with a pull the spring scale can measure, and exactly what does that machine cost us in distance?
to: Which approved tabletop machine lets us lift the same model load with less measured force, and how much farther does the effort travel?

from.context: Movers needed to get a piano into a truck bed a meter off the ground.
from.move: They laid a long ramp instead of lifting, then added a rope around a pulley on the truck so two people could pull from the truck bed. They accepted walking the piano four meters to gain one meter of height, and they waxed the ramp to cut friction.
from.whyItHelps: It is the same trade with the same two fixes you can use: a longer path for less force, and a pulley to change direction. Waxing the ramp is the friction fee being paid on purpose.

to.context: A team needed to raise a small sealed model container onto a block.
to.move: They compared two ramps that reached the same 8-centimeter height. They pulled the same model steadily with a newton scale, recorded force and travel distance, and repeated each test. The longer ramp was predicted to need less pull; friction could change the measured values.
to.whyItHelps: The load and rise stayed constant while ramp length changed, making the comparison useful.
